papers.title: Buried Interfacial Transport Governs Oxide-Protected Electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: Abstract Protective overlayers are widely used to stabilize metal catalysts under harsh electrochemical conditions. Unlike graphene coatings, oxide overlayers introduce a buried metal-oxide interface that fundamentally reshapes reaction pathways by separating proton delivery from product release. Although proton transport through oxides has been extensively investigated, the fate of reaction products at buried interfaces remains unresolved; for example, H2-molecule vs H-atom pathways remain under debate in oxide-protected hydrogen evolution. Here, we revisit this buried interface using a microelectrochemical cell with well-defined model structures. Systematic measurements across nine metal-oxide heterostructures, combined with density functional theory calculations, reveal that product transport is governed by two sequential kinetic barriers: hydrogen spillover across the metal-oxide junction and hydrogen permeation through the oxide lattice. These coupled barriers determine whether reaction products are released, accumulate at buried interfaces, or induce interfacial failure. This work not only identifies superior Pt-TiO2 and Pd-TiO2 but also clarifies which step is impeded in Au-TiO2, Pt-SiO2, Pt-HfO2, Pd-SiO2, Pd-HfO2, Au-SiO2, and Au-HfO2 heterostructures. Guided by these model studies, we implement a TiO2 protection strategy in a proton-exchange-membrane water electrolyzer with remarkable durability. These findings provide a framework for constructing a complete proton-to-product route for buried interfaces, potentially resolving long-standing ambiguities in oxide-protected electrocatalysis.

papers.title: Regulating Functionalized MXene Crystal-Field Splitting toward Efficient Bifunctional Oxygen Electrocatalysis of Lithium–Oxygen Batteries
papers.abstract: Abstract MXenes offer fast conductive frameworks with abundant intrinsic active metal sites, making them promising cathode catalysts for lithium–oxygen batteries for addressing sluggish oxygen kinetics and severe cathode passivation. However, the predictive electronic descriptors for rationally regulating these intrinsic active sites remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate the implementation of crystal-field splitting engineering at Ti sites of Ti3C2-MXene to achieve bifunctional oxygen electrocatalysis. Through coordinated anionic and cationic modifications, we regulate the local coordination environment of Ti atoms, weakening crystal-field splitting and promoting electron delocalization within Ti3C2-MXene frameworks. X-ray absorption spectra reveal systematic shifts of Ti K-edge and contraction of the pre-edge splitting, consistent with weakened and distorted Ti ligand fields. This electronic rearrangement promotes an asymmetric Li2O2 adsorption configuration, thereby lowering the energy barriers for both ORR and OER. Consequently, the functionalized Cu–Ti3C2Br2 delivers a high discharge specific capacity of 11,662 mAh g–1 and reduces the initial charge overpotential by 50% compared with Ti3C2OF. This study indicates crystal-field splitting as a key descriptor governing oxygen electrocatalytic behavior in lithium–oxygen batteries.

papers.title: Zeolite Crystallization via Seed-Mediated Chemical Vapor Deposition
papers.abstract: Abstract The demand for zeolites with specific, tailored characteristics is expected to further accelerate. For decades, however, zeolites have been predominantly synthesized by hydrothermal methods, in which tightly coupled sol–gel processes, nucleation, and crystal growth constrain property control and complicate device-oriented fabrication. Here we report the direct synthesis of zeolites by chemical vapor deposition (CVD), in which vapor-delivered precursors crystallize on preexisting zeolite seeds. Mechanistic investigations reveal that zeolite growth under CVD follows a fundamentally distinct pathway, where vapor-phase hydrolysis–condensation reactions are spatially decoupled from interfacial crystallization. This decoupling enables the maintenance of a controlled and steady supersaturation, offering a facile strategy for fabricating zeolite films with low dielectric constants and robust mechanical properties. The unique mechanism and operation mode of CVD bring zeolite crystallization into a manufacturing-relevant vapor-phase regime that could be extended to other zeolite types and deployed in diverse applications.

papers.title: Proton-Coupled Electrostatic Regulation of Anion Electrosorption in Electric Double Layers
papers.abstract: Abstract Electric double layers underpin electrochemical energy storage and modulate interfacial reactivity through the organization of ions and solvent molecules. However, regulating anion accumulation at compact aqueous interfaces while limiting parasitic water reactions remains challenging. Here, anodic polarization reconstructs oxygen-deficient TiO2–x into a depth-graded architecture comprising a rutile interior, a disordered interlayer, and a thin crystalline anatase surface. This architecture establishes an internal electric field that promotes subsurface proton accumulation, creating a responsive charge distribution that regulates anion electrosorption and moderates lateral anion interactions. The thin crystalline surface complements this electrostatic regulation by extending the accessible anodic operating range, combining enhanced interfacial charge storage with high-voltage aqueous operation. Symmetric aqueous supercapacitors sustain cycling over 3.0 V in neutral Na2SO4 for 45,000 cycles and over 2.7 V in natural seawater. These findings identify subsurface ionic chemistry as a design variable for regulating anion electrosorption at aqueous oxide interfaces.

papers.title: Thiol-ene Radical Polymerizations of Regio - and Stereo -Isomers of a CO2-Derived δ-Lactone Leading to High Molar Mass Polythioethers
papers.abstract: Abstract Thiol-ene radical polymerization of CO2-derived lactones containing α,δ-dienes offers a route to sustainable polythioethers with up to 20 wt % CO2. The direct product from CO2/1,3-butadiene telomerization is 3-ethylidene-6-vinyltetrahydro-2H-pyran-2-one ((E)EVP) whose α-alkylidene group causes poor reaction kinetics and nonquantitative alkene conversion with dithiols affording low molar mass polythioethers. Here, we use 3,6-divinyltetrahydro-2H-pyran-2-one (DVP) which was synthesized from the base-catalyzed contrathermodynamic α,β- to β,γ-photodeconjugation of EVP, resulting in the transformation of the α-alkylidene to an α-vinyl functional group. This subtle regio-isomerization was found to result in a 17-fold and 8-fold increase in the rate of α- and δ-ene consumption, respectively, owing to the relative stability of the intermediate carbon-centered radicals. Leveraging these rapid kinetics, high molar mass polythioethers (34 kDa) could be prepared via thiol-ene step-growth polymerization of DVP with 2,2’-(ethylenedioxy)diethanethiol. These molar masses are 10-fold higher than the upper limits obtained with the EVP-derived counterpart, and the polythioethers display mechanical performance suitable as a pressure sensitive adhesive.

papers.title: Detecting Catalytically Competent Surface-Bound Hydrogen on Electrocatalysts with Weak Acids
papers.abstract: Abstract The characterization of catalytically competent molecular metal-hydride intermediates distinguishes mechanistic possibilities in reductive molecular electrocatalysis. While surface-bound hydrogen is invoked in several heterogeneous electrocatalytic schemes, the synthetic and spectroscopic tools to establish catalytic competence in molecular systems are not readily translated to surfaces. Molecular systems offer uniform and well-defined active sites; however, surface systems consist of multiple possible binding sites. Here, we discover that the judicious choice of the proton donor enables the independent generation and characterization of catalytically competent surface-bound hydrogen using hydrogen evolution as a model reaction. Using dimethyl sulfoxide, a solvent where Brønsted acid pKa values are well-characterized, and Ag electrocatalysts, compatible with surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (SEIRAS), we find that acids with pKa values higher than the protonated solvent generate spectroscopic signatures consistent with the reductive formation of long-lived and linearly bound hydrogen. Conversely, stronger acids that protonate the solvent do not give rise to detectable surface-bound hydrogen, and instead, yield electrokinetic data consistent with hydrogen evolution proceeding via rate-limiting formation of the same linearly bound surface hydrogen. By independently generating the Ag-bound hydrogen with a weak, general acid and subsequently introducing a stronger acid that protonates the solvent, we show that the accumulated surface-bound hydrogen is catalytically competent for hydrogen production via specific-acid-coupled electron transfer. Our work demonstrates that catalytically competent surface-bound hydrogen intermediates in heterogeneous electrocatalysis can be detected and characterized through the strategic choice of the proton donor.

papers.title: Directional Nitrite Spillover Couples to Interfacial Hydrogen-Bond Networks for Ampere-Level Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electrosynthesis
papers.abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia is often constrained by the proton-coupled hydrogenation of adsorbed nitrite (*NO2), a step commonly accelerated through hydrogen spillover and local reactive-hydrogen (*H) supply. This hydrogen-centered view, however, treats *NO2 largely as a passive intermediate and overlooks whether its migration can reconstruct the interfacial hydrogen-bond-network environment required for downstream hydrogenation. Here, we show that directional *NO2 spillover couples site-specific intermediate transport with interfacial hydrogen-bond-network reorganization. In a Cu–Ag dual-site model interface, nitrate activation and *NO2 formation occur preferentially on the Cu sites, whereas migrated *NO2 species are stabilized and hydrogenated on the Ag-associated sites. In situ spectroscopy, kinetic isotope measurements, distribution-of-relaxation-time analysis, and theoretical simulations reveal that this Cu-to-Ag relay enriches K+-associated interfacial water, reinforces hydrogen-bond connectivity, and facilitates *H delivery for *NO2 hydrogenation. The optimized CuAg N-doped carbon (CuAg–N-C) achieves near-unity Faradaic efficiency (FE) for NH3 with a yield rate of 411.8 mmol g–1 h–1 and retains 83% FE at 1 A cm–2 in a flow cell. The catalyst further retains substantial nitrate-to-ammonia recovery in simulated and authentic industrial water matrices. More broadly, this work establishes *NO2 spillover as a dynamic interfacial mechanism linking intermediate transport, water-network organization, and proton-coupled nitrogen conversion, providing a framework for sustaining molecular-scale selectivity under chemically complex reaction environments.

papers.title: Secondary Solvation Shell Regulation for Fast-Charging Lithium Metal Batteries
papers.abstract: Abstract Most electrolyte strategies in lithium metal batteries (LMBs) target the first solvation shell or solvation diversity. However, such approaches have shown limited success in enabling fast-charging, as Li+ depletion inevitably develops at polarized interfaces. Here, we identify the secondary solvation shell as a critical regulator of fast-charging stability and show that a gradient solvation structure (GSS) overcomes ion depletion-induced failure. Guided by intrinsic solvation strengths, we design a tri-solvent electrolyte comprising 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME), 1,1,1-trifluoro-2,3-dimethoxypropane (TFDMP), and N,N-dimethyltrifluoromethane-sulfonamide (DMTMSA). DME and TFDMP define a stable primary solvation shell and balanced ion-pair distribution, whereas DMTMSA localizes in the secondary shell, suppressing long-range ionic clustering and maintaining interfacial ion availability. Despite similar primary-shell structures and equilibrium impedances, only the tri-solvent system preserves interfacial kinetics under depletion conditions. This architecture enables a Coulombic efficiency of 98.4% at 16 mA cm–2, a specific capacity of 162.0 mAh g–1 at 10C, and 90.4% capacity retention for 200 cycles. These findings establish a gradient solvation structure as a governing principle for fast-charging LMB electrolytes.

papers.title: Unraveling the Intrinsic Interfacial Chemistry of Fluoroethylene Carbonate on Lithium Metal Anodes via a Solvent-Free Model System
papers.abstract: Abstract Fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) is a widely used film-forming additive for stabilizing lithium metal anodes (LMAs), yet its intrinsic interfacial chemistry remains elusive because its reactions are coupled with those of solvents and Li salts in conventional electrolytes. Herein, a solvent-free, dry-processed poly(ethylene oxide)-based solid polymer electrolyte (PEO@Dry) is developed as a platform to isolate the interfacial reactions of FEC without interference from traditional liquid organic solvents. PEO@Dry retains the intrinsic interfacial reactivity of PEO and LiTFSI while eliminating solvent-derived interference. FEC is found to undergo a spontaneous chemical reaction with Li metal before electrochemical reduction, producing a dense LiF-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) that is subsequently reinforced by organic species derived from the electrochemical reactions. The resulting SEI exhibits a well-defined composition and robust structure, leading to an enhanced interfacial stability and electrochemical performance. Comparative research with a DME-based liquid electrolyte reveals that FEC (DME@FEC) follows distinct reaction pathways depending on its solvation state. In the solvent-free PEO@Dry system, free FEC undergoes sequential chemical and electrochemical reduction to form an inorganic-rich SEI, whereas in the liquid electrolyte, FEC participates in Li+ solvation and competes with other electrolyte components, yielding a more complex SEI. This work clarifies the interfacial mechanism of FEC and establishes a general solvent-free platform for mechanistic studies of electrolyte additives on LMAs.

papers.title: Zero-excess sodium-metal batteries for post-lithium energy storage
papers.abstract: Nature Reviews Clean Technology, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s44359-026-00234-6 Zero-excess sodium-metal batteries combine high energy density, resource abundance and simplified manufacturing, positioning them as a potential post-lithium energy-storage technology. This Review examines the promise of this technology, the failure mechanisms and design principles of zero-excess sodium-metal batteries, and their deployment readiness.

papers.title: Set efficiency criteria for access to geological carbon dioxide storage
papers.abstract: Nature Reviews Clean Technology, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s44359-026-00237-3 Geological CO2 storage sites are critical to achieving climate-relevant carbon sequestration. Efficiency metrics should be used to ensure that limited storage capacity is not used on CO2 from capture projects with high levels of life-cycle carbon emissions.

papers.title: Challenges and requirements for lithium–oxygen batteries
papers.abstract: Nature Reviews Clean Technology, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s44359-026-00222-w Lithium–oxygen batteries promise high energy density, but poor reversibility and limited cycle life continue to hinder their development. This Review examines component and configuration challenges, scalability, economics, and environmental impacts and end-of-life recycling implications.
